b2: Still, I wouldn't write off genuine feelings about who you're attracted to, or your gender, as "just intrusive thoughts" only because they're confusing or unwanted. Or because the people around you would disapprove (I'm not pushing anyone toward or away from any orientation or gender). Nobody has to settle it now, and what you do in the meantime can go by what you care about. What keeps coming back in your own experience over time tells you more, even if you've kept it out of your life so far. Whichever passing feeling is loudest isn't automatically the "real you", and neither is what a therapist or anyone else says it means.
f1: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening. It might really be warning you about overload or humiliation. Or danger, or a boundary. But a part can be trying to protect you from something that won't happen, and you can listen to it without obeying it. With most decisions there's a way to find out. What did it say would happen, and what actually happened? Sometimes it was right, too. If it might be danger right now, though, or something in your body a doctor should see, I'd handle that first and check later whether the anxiety was right.
f2: Some of it I wouldn't test at all, even when it sounds like a prediction. If a part hesitates about being touched or about sex, that's enough to stop. Same with going deeper in this work, or an altered state. That isn't something to test. It might not be able to tell you why.
d1: Turning the depth down like that isn't giving up on the relationship with your little one. Unless it's the inner child idea itself that you don't want, and maybe you've half known it for a while. Then it's not a pacing problem, and none of my pacing advice overrides that choice. Drop the language, and don't bring it back in through some "gentler" exercise or by calling everyday tasks reparenting. Care and protection still go on, in whatever words fit you. So do guidance and other people's support.
d2: If you do want the relationship but the depth you're at is too much, change the dose. During an exercise you might think, "I'm not sure I could stop this and come back if I had to." Or you've lost track of where you are, or going inward is itself making things worse. Then stop the exercise and turn outward first. Don't try another inward technique to prove you can take it. When you're steadier, the next gentlest step might be something protective out in your life, or real support from a person. Or a short eyes-open hello to your little one, before any imagery or deeper talk.
d3: A full pause is the last resort, though a safety problem can force one on you. It still doesn't mean the relationship failed. Make it specific. What made it necessary, and what was the last level that was really workable? What visible change, plus your own say-so, would make a gentle return reasonable? Wait for that. You might wonder if you're ready yet, but don't keep testing lighter versions with your little one in the meantime, not even just picturing them. Come back at or below that last workable level. And if an earlier session was hard and you haven't checked how it landed yet, do that before stepping up again.
p1: Whatever you pick from that map, don't judge whether a session was safe by how pleasant it felt. A session that's doing you good can still bring up grief and fear. There can be hard dreams too, or stuff you'd really rather not meet. A session can be hard without harming you, and an intense one might not have gotten you anywhere. Even "I stayed present" isn't enough by itself. What tells you more is whether you could stop and come back to the room. Then there's whether you actually want to go back toward what came up.
p2: Did it feel hard but workable, or just too much? Notice how you slept and how you got through the days after. If you don't know yet, don't rush to call it healing or harm. Ask yourself how it landed, then adjust the challenge. While you're finding your level, change one thing at a time so you learn what matters. If your distress is climbing, or you've been less able to function since, change several at once. Make it shorter, with less depth or imagery. Pick a better time of day, and get more support around you. Keep your eyes open, even if that feels like cheating.
p3: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. If you're not sure yet whether you want to, you can wait. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. Dreams and imagery that come up can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.
i1: If being alone is part of the wound, reaching toward people can be one way the grown-up you takes care of your little one. You can call that reparenting if the inner-child language fits. If it doesn't, you don't need to. A decent parent wouldn't tell a lonely kid to become totally self-sufficient before they can see their friends. Sometimes the grown-up move is calling someone. Maybe you already know who. Or it's setting up a visit, or asking a social worker what's out there. Maybe it's getting yourself into a room where people share something real.
i2: Look for more than one door. Who do you already trust? Which friendships go both ways? You could take a class, or volunteer. A spiritual community counts too, if it really fits you. Branching out is no reason to drop somebody good. Not every door has to open, either. Several imperfect supports usually hold up better than one partner or therapist being the only place you belong. Bring the Protector along too. Belonging doesn't make a group good, even when you finally feel wanted there. A high-control group isn't "support" to lean into. Neither is someone in authority who exploits people, or a relationship where you've actually been hurt or threatened.
